title: China Completes World's Largest Fusion Magnet, Advancing Its Artificial Sun Program
excerpt: The 582-tonne superconducting magnet stores three times the energy of its ITER counterpart and was built entirely with domestic technology.
body:
• China has completed testing of the world's largest superconducting magnet for nuclear fusion, weighing 582 tonnes and measuring 21 metres long
  • The toroidal-field coil stores three times the energy and has 1.3 times the volume of the equivalent magnet at the ITER reactor in France
  • All critical components — speciality steel, insulation, and superconducting wires — were manufactured domestically, marking 100% indigenous production
  • Sixteen of these coils will eventually form a magnetic cage capable of confining plasma hotter than 100 million degrees Celsius

China has successfully completed performance testing of the world's largest superconducting magnet for a nuclear fusion reactor, clearing a critical engineering milestone in its quest to build an "artificial sun" that replicates the energy-producing reaction at the heart of real stars.

The toroidal-field coil, built for the Comprehensive Research Facility for Fusion Technology (CRAFT) project in Hefei, stands 21 metres long, 12 metres wide, and 3.3 metres high. At 582 tonnes, it weighs more than four adult blue whales. The magnet passed comprehensive acceptance by an expert panel on June 27, according to the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Plasma Physics (ASIPP).

Surpassing International Benchmarks

The achievement puts China ahead of the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER), the multinational fusion project under construction in southern France that has faced years of delays and cost overruns. China's CRAFT magnet has 1.3 times the volume and three times the energy storage capacity of ITER's equivalent component.

"This is currently the world's largest fully superconducting coil in terms of weight and the highest in stored energy."

— Song Yuntao, Director, Institute of Plasma Physics, ASIPP

The magnet's job is deceptively simple in concept but extraordinarily difficult in execution: it must generate an invisible magnetic cage strong enough to contain plasma heated past 100 million degrees Celsius — over six times hotter than the core of the sun. No physical material can withstand such temperatures, so the magnetic field guides charged particles along prescribed paths, keeping them away from the reactor walls.

Six Years of Indigenous Development

Song Yuntao, the institute's director, said the magnet took six years to complete and represents a fully indigenous achievement. The speciality stainless steel, insulation materials, and superconducting wires were all manufactured in China, achieving what the institute calls "100 percent domestic manufacturing" across the entire production chain.

On the same day, a second critical component — a high-temperature superconducting central solenoid coil — also completed full-condition parameter testing. The central solenoid is responsible for initiating and controlling the plasma current inside the reactor. It was designed for a rated current of 46.5 kiloamperes but successfully passed testing at 60 kiloamperes.

Global Fusion Race Intensifies

The breakthrough comes as the global race for commercial fusion energy accelerates. While ITER has struggled with construction delays and a budget that has ballooned past €20 billion, China has been steadily advancing its own fusion program. The country's Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST) set a record in 2025 by holding superheated plasma steady for 1,066 seconds.

In the CRAFT reactor's final configuration, 16 of the massive toroidal-field coils will be assembled into a ring, each carrying 100 kiloamperes and generating a magnetic field of 6.5 tesla at the centre — strong enough to confine the miniature star indefinitely.

What It Means for India and the World

India is a member of the ITER consortium and has contributed key components to the French project. China's rapid progress raises strategic questions about whether India's fusion investment — channelled primarily through its ITER participation — remains the most effective path. Indian scientists at the Institute for Plasma Research in Gujarat have been developing their own tokamak experiments, but China's demonstrated ability to build reactor-scale components entirely in-house shifts the competitive landscape significantly.

What's Next

A working fusion power plant remains years away, but clearing the magnet hurdle eliminates one of the most difficult engineering challenges on the path to commercial fusion. ASIPP researchers say the next phase involves assembling the full magnetic system and integrating it with the CRAFT tokamak vessel. If successful, CRAFT would become the world's most advanced fusion research facility, potentially putting China in a position to build a prototype fusion power plant before any other nation.
